notes.meaning: David cries out to God while hiding in the dry, barren desert of Judah. Even though he is far away from the tabernacle, his whole body and soul thirst for God more than for water. He seeks the Lord eagerly at the start of each day because nothing in this world can satisfy him like God can.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: In Orthodox tradition, this is counted as Psalm 62 and is chanted every morning at the beginning of the Matins service as one of the Six Psalms.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the dry desert not as a real wilderness where David was running from enemies, but as a poetic picture of an exile who misses the temple.

notes.meaning: David remembers the times he visited God's sanctuary, the holy place of public worship. There he had seen God's power and majesty at work among His people. Even though he is now stuck in the wilderness, he looks to God in his heart and longs to experience that holy presence once again.

God's faithful, covenant love means more to David than life itself. Earthly life will end, but God's merciful kindness lasts forever and brings true spiritual life. Because David knows this great love, he cannot stay quiet and chooses to praise God with his lips.

differ.view: Reformed teachers note that the word for life is plural in Hebrew, showing that God's loving mercy sustains believers even in the face of death, proving far greater than worldly prosperity.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early writer Augustine noted that the ancient text uses the plural word lives, arguing that God's one promised life of grace is far better than the many worldly careers people pursue.

notes.meaning: David promises to honor and thank God as long as he lives. Lifting up hands was a traditional way to pray, showing open hands ready to receive from God and surrender to Him. Honoring the Lord's name will be David's daily work through every trial.

differ.view: Many charismatics teach that lifting hands is an active biblical pattern for worship that expresses personal surrender and full dependence on God.
Many Baptists teach that lifting hands is an optional posture, emphasizing that an upright and holy heart matters far more in prayer than physical gestures.

notes.meaning: Being close to God satisfies David like the richest, most delicious banquet. Even while facing hunger in a lonely desert, his soul feels completely full and cared for by the Lord. This deep inner peace makes his mouth burst into joyful singing.

David lies awake at night and turns his attention to God instead of worrying. During the quiet night hours, he meditates, which means he carefully thinks over God's promises and goodness. Remembering God's care brings peace to his mind through dark and lonely times.

David looks back on how God has rescued him many times before. He pictures himself resting under God's protective wings, like a little chick sheltered by its mother. Remembering past help gives him confidence to sing with joy about what lies ahead.

David clings closely to the Lord, following Him step by step with all his strength. Yet he knows that he only stays standing because God's strong right hand is holding him up. Believers hold on to God only because God is faithfully holding on to them.

David turns to the enemies who are actively hunting him down to take his life. He knows their wicked plans will fail and lead to their own destruction in the place of the dead. God will defend His servant and bring righteous judgment on those who do evil.

Those who fight against God's chosen leader will fall in battle by the sword. Instead of receiving a peaceful burial, their bodies will be left in the wilderness for scavenging animals like wild jackals. This shows the tragic and shameful end of opposing the Lord.

David rejoices because God will honor His promise and keep him safe as king. Everyone who sincerely worships the Lord and stays loyal to Him will share in this great victory. Meanwhile, the mouths of treacherous liars will be completely shut forever.
